Dear Area Chair and Reviewers,

We have just uploaded a revised version of the manuscript to the system. We have made thorough revisions to address all the comments and suggestions raised during the review process, including adding new baselines, expanding experimental scope, and clarifying key concepts.

We believe these changes significantly strengthen the paper and address the concerns raised during the discussion period. Thank you again for your constructive guidance. We sincerely appreciate your time and effort in helping us improve our work.

Sincerely,

The Authors

Dear Reviewer TRCD,

Thank you so much for providing this detailed and critical review. We sincerely appreciate the time you have taken to provide this feedback. We hope the following point-to-point response can address your concerns.

---

**Q1.** The manuscript is kind of overloaded.

**A1.** Thank you for the insightful and constructive feedback. We agree that focusing on the core topological findings strengthens the paper. Consequently, during this rebuttal phase, we have prioritized our primary contribution, graph probing, significantly expanding our experiments in this area.

Specifically, we have extended our analysis to include a wider range of semantics, probing neural topology to predict time and space context of the input text following previous literature (Gurnee & Tegmark, 2024), and demonstrating the generalization of our graph probing framework. We utilized the same datasets of historical-artworks and world-places as in (Gurnee & Tegmark, 2024), constructing the neural topology and predicting the release time of the artwork and the longitute/latitude of the places. The results are summarized in the following table,


| LLM | Probe | Arts (time) MSE | Arts (time) MAE | Arts (time) R² | World Places (space) MSE | World Places (space) MAE | World Places (space) R² |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **GPT-2** | Activation (Linear) | 0.0433 | 0.1660 | 0.2489 | 0.0353 | 0.1906 | 0.5189 |
| | Activation (MLP) | 0.0433 | 0.1665 | 0.2483 | 0.0358 | 0.1922 | 0.5130 |
| | **Graph (Linear)** | **0.0326** | **0.1371** | **0.4341** | **0.0317** | **0.1765** | **0.5689** |
| | **Graph (MLP)** | **0.0267** | **0.1230** | **0.5361** | **0.0258** | **0.1514** | **0.6486** |
| **Pythia-160M** | Activation (Linear) | 0.0438 | 0.1664 | 0.2391 | 0.0349 | 0.1896 | 0.5238 |
| | Activation (MLP) | 0.0439 | 0.1661 | 0.2382 | 0.0312 | 0.1726 | 0.5724 |
| | **Graph (Linear)** | **0.0282** | **0.1275** | **0.5100** | **0.0267** | **0.1583** | **0.6335** |
| | **Graph (MLP)** | **0.0266** | **0.1234** | **0.5387** | **0.0246** | **0.1447** | **0.6636** |
| **Qwen2.5-0.5B** | Activation (Linear) | 0.0350 | 0.1472 | 0.3930 | 0.0320 | 0.1801 | 0.5676 |
| | Activation (MLP) | 0.0346 | 0.1463 | 0.4001 | 0.0268 | 0.1541 | 0.6323 |
| | **Graph (Linear)** | **0.0258** | **0.1221** | **0.5524** | **0.0215** | **0.1364** | **0.7080** |
| | **Graph (MLP)** | **0.0268** | **0.1254** | **0.5341** | **0.0223** | **0.1398** | **0.6953** |

We can observe that graph probing still significantly outperforms baselines probing on activations. For example, the improvements of graph probing against baselines exceed 40.55% and 24.73% on time and space datasets respectively for the Qwen2.5 model. These additional results not only validate the findings from previous work that LLMs represent time and space internally, but more importantly confirm that neural topology contains much richer information than neural activation which can be effectively captured by graph probing.

We believe these additions successfully provide the rigorous validation and detailed interpretation as you requested. 

---
**Q2.** Relationship between graph probing and hub neurons

**A2.** Thank you for this interesting question regarding the structural alignment between the connections identified by graph probing and hub neurons. We would like to highlight the sparsity experiments illustrated in Figure 3(a). These results verify that retaining only the top 10%, or even just 1%, of the strongest connections allows us to predict model perplexity with high accuracy. Specifically, using only these important connections incurs a performance drop of less than 5% in the perplexity regression task. In this context, where only the most significant edges are retained, the definitions of topological importance and "hub-ness" are exactly the same, implying the overlap between important nodes identified by graph probing and hub nodes.

Dear Reviewer SqX2,

Thank you for the quick and engaging follow-up. We genuinely appreciate your push for a deeper mechanistic connection. To address your concern of how a specific neuron-neuron interaction drives model behavior, we conducted an additional "minimal intervention" experiment during this short window.

Bisides the massive pruning experiment in the original paper which changes global statistics, we performed precise surgical interventions on the OpenWebText dataset. Specifically, we identified neurons based on our neural topology (highest degree vs. lowest degree). Then we "disabled" the interactions of these specific neurons. We tested two minimal cases: (1) Num=1: We disabled the connections of the single most connected (Top-1 Interaction Disabled) or least connected (Bottom-1 Interaction Disabled) neuron to its neighbors. (2) Num=2: We disabled the connections for the top-2 vs. bottom-2 neurons.

If the topology is just a byproduct, interfering with "high-degree" interactions should not be drastically different from "low-degree" ones, or at least not catastrophic. If the topology represents a load-bearing functional circuit, breaking the "hubs" of interaction should disproportionately hurt performance. The loss on the OpenWebText dataset for the original and intervened LLMs are shown in the table below.

| Model | Original Loss | Top-1 Interaction Disabled | Bottom-1 Interaction Disabled | Top-2 Interactions Disabled | Bottom-2 Interactions Disabled |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **GPT-2** | 3.0944 | 3.1324 (+0.0380) | 3.0963 (+0.0019) | 3.2915 (+0.1971) | 3.0975 (+0.0031) |
| **Pythia-160M** | 3.1777 | 3.1813 (+0.0036) | 3.1784 (+0.0007) | 3.1851 (+0.0074) | 3.1791 (+0.0014) |
| **Qwen2.5-0.5B** | 2.9182 | 4.7223 (+1.8041) | 2.9193 (+0.0011) | 4.8602 (+1.9420) | 2.9206 (+0.0024) |


The results provide striking causal evidence on the influence of specific neuron-neuron correlation. Specifically, the impact of the "hub" neuron is orders of magnitude higher than the "non-hub" neuron. For example, disabling the interactions of just one hub neuron causes the loss increment to explode from 0.0011 to 1.8041 for Qwen2.5-0.5B, which is more than 1640 times. For GPT-2, the loss increase for the top neuron is ~20x higher than the bottom one. For Pythia, it is over 5x higher.


This confirms that the specific neuron-neuron interactions identified by our graph are not merely correlational byproducts but are causally necessary for the model's computation. The model relies on these specific high-interaction pathways for text generation of high quality. 

We believe this directly answers your call to show how specific interactions drive model behavior. Thank you again for raising your score.

Sincerely,

The Authors

Dear Reviewer SqX2,

Thank you so much for providing this detailed and critical review. We sincerely appreciate the time you have taken to provide this feedback. We hope the following point-to-point response can address your concerns.

---

**Q1.** Unclear purpose of proposed method.

**A1.** Thank you for your critical feedback. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify the fundamental motivation and contribution of our work.

1. **The shift from activation to topology.** The primary contribution of our paper is to propose a new "object" for analysis: neural topology, distinct from the traditional focus on neural activation. While standard probing links activations to semantics, our goal is to demonstrate that the interactions between neurons (the dynamic graph structure) contain unique, high-level information that raw activations alone do not capture. We adopted perplexity and hallucination as initial probing targets because they are direct, holistic indicators of an LLM's performance on language understanding and generation, making them suitable proxies for evaluating the informational content of the topology.
2. **New experiments on space and time (aligning with prior work).** We totally agree with your comment regarding the selection of probing targets. To address this and better align our work with the established interpretability literature, we conducted extensive additional experiments during this rebuttal phase. Specifically, we adopted the space and time datasets utilized by Gurnee & Tegmark (2024). We constructed the neural topology for input texts regarding historical artworks and world places, and trained probes to predict: (1) Time: The release year of historical artworks. (2) Space: The longitude and latitude of world places. The results are summarized in the table below. We observe that graph probing significantly outperforms baselines that probe on activations.

| LLM | Probe | Arts (time) MSE | Arts (time) MAE | Arts (time) R² | World Places (space) MSE | World Places (space) MAE | World Places (space) R² |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **GPT-2** | Activation (Linear) | 0.0433 | 0.1660 | 0.2489 | 0.0353 | 0.1906 | 0.5189 |
| | Activation (MLP) | 0.0433 | 0.1665 | 0.2483 | 0.0358 | 0.1922 | 0.5130 |
| | **Graph (Linear)** | **0.0326** | **0.1371** | **0.4341** | **0.0317** | **0.1765** | **0.5689** |
| | **Graph (MLP)** | **0.0267** | **0.1230** | **0.5361** | **0.0258** | **0.1514** | **0.6486** |
| **Pythia-160M** | Activation (Linear) | 0.0438 | 0.1664 | 0.2391 | 0.0349 | 0.1896 | 0.5238 |
| | Activation (MLP) | 0.0439 | 0.1661 | 0.2382 | 0.0312 | 0.1726 | 0.5724 |
| | **Graph (Linear)** | **0.0282** | **0.1275** | **0.5100** | **0.0267** | **0.1583** | **0.6335** |
| | **Graph (MLP)** | **0.0266** | **0.1234** | **0.5387** | **0.0246** | **0.1447** | **0.6636** |
| **Qwen2.5-0.5B** | Activation (Linear) | 0.0350 | 0.1472 | 0.3930 | 0.0320 | 0.1801 | 0.5676 |
| | Activation (MLP) | 0.0346 | 0.1463 | 0.4001 | 0.0268 | 0.1541 | 0.6323 |
| | **Graph (Linear)** | **0.0258** | **0.1221** | **0.5524** | **0.0215** | **0.1364** | **0.7080** |
| | **Graph (MLP)** | **0.0268** | **0.1254** | **0.5341** | **0.0223** | **0.1398** | **0.6953** |

These additional results serve two critical purposes:
1.	They validate findings from previous work showing that LLMs possess internal representations of time and space.
2.	Crucially, they confirm that neural topology contains significantly richer information than neural activation for these semantic tasks. The substantial performance margin suggests that the structure of computation (how neurons connect) is more predictive than the magnitude of computation (activations) for extracting high-level concepts.


We believe these findings directly address your concern by demonstrating that our method can indeed link model structure to interpretable semantics (time and space) more effectively than traditional methods. For baselines and hallucination experiments, please refer to our response to the next point.

**Q6.** Overstatement.

**A6.** We agree that some of our initial interpretations were overstated. We have revised the manuscript to tune down these statements, removing the strong analogies to the biological Default Mode Network and tempering the claims regarding linear separability. Our updated text focuses on reporting the empirical stability of hub neurons and the observable clustering trends, ensuring the discussion emphasizes the key technical contributions of the paper without overreaching.

---

Thank you again for your engagement and valuable questions, which have helped us improve the clarity of our paper. If our responses and the new experiments have resolved your concerns, we would be very grateful if you would consider raising your score. We are, of course, happy to address any further questions you may have.



Sincerely,

The Authors

summary.value: This paper introduces a new method for probing, inspired by methods in neuroscience. Using this new method, which they term *graph probing*, one computes the pairwise Pearson correlations between neurons across timesteps, and feeds this into a linear or MLP probe. Using this method, the authors are able to more successfully probe for quantities like model perplexity on a sequence, as compared to standard probes. Interpreting the values in the correlation matrix as a graph, they also find hub neurons (those with high degree), and show that ablating these disproportionately hurts model performance, indicating their functional importance. They finally use these probes for pruning, hallucination detection, and model fingerprinting.

strengths.value: This paper is well-written and polished: the text is clear, and the graphs are well-constructed. I also think that this particularly style of probing is novel: I haven't heard of others using it before.

weaknesses.value:
**Unclear Purpose of Proposed Method**: The primary use of probing in interpretability is, as noted by this paper, "linking neural activations to interpretable semantics". But this paper never actually does this, which is the one thing that one would expect from a probing paper. In fact, since it's restricted to sequence-level probing, it can't do many probing tasks, which are often token-level. 

Instead, it probes for things like perplexity (why would you want a probe to predict that?) and uses probes to identify important neurons (we know that such neurons exist, and don't need probes to find them), identify hallucinations (this is useful, but there's a lot of past work to compare to), and model fingerprinting (same issue). Ultimately, an interpretability method should help us understand better how models work, but I don't think this paper does so; instead, it focuses on applications that appear useful on the surface, but are hamstrung by insufficient baselines / connection to prior work. In doing so, it ends up in an awkward position where it doesn't make a very novel or significant contribution to either model interpretability or capabilities. 

**Weak Evaluation / Insufficient Baselines**: This paper doesn't perform enough / the right baselines, making its results less sound:
- For the probing for perplexity experiments, the baseline probes only receive the last token representation. You should give them something that combines information from all of the positions; it doesn't make sense to baseline against a method that receives so much less information in its input.
- For the pruning experiments, why not compare to any other pruning methods? If the point of this method is to be useful, then it should really be more useful than alternatives.
- Ditto for the hallucination experiments.
- Ditto again for the model fingerprinting experiments. I'd also love more discussion about how / whether the Pythia experiments really reflect a real-world fingerprinting use-case. 

**Relation to prior work**: This paper actually cites a lot of prior work! But I think that it misses out on some crucial work that would provide context. For example: 
- this paper stresses the finding of so-called hub neurons, but it is well-known that neurons vary in importance with respect to individual tasks; see [Vig and Belinkov](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2020/hash/92650b2e92217715fe312e6fa7b90d82-Abstract.html) who find that just a few neurons matter for a gender bias task. For papers looking at this from a more general POV, see [Timkey et al](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.372/), who investigate neurons whose activations are very high-magnitude, and [Dettmers et al](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339), who find that not quantizing these neurons is important, as doing so hurts model performance. It follows fairly naturally that zero ablating these - a much more destructive intervention than quantization - will hurt model performance as well. The authors push this "hub neuron" / "default network" narrative very hard, but these findings are already known, and the neuro connection seems forced.
- Where is the related work on pruning / hallucinations / model fingerprinting? For the first two cases, there has been tons of interp work to compare to. 
- Re: probing, please cite work from before 2022! There is a lot of thoughtful probing literature that predates probing in mech interp; indeed, a lot of that probing literature is better than what has emerged recently. You can look at [BERTology](https://aclanthology.org/2020.tacl-1.54/) for classic probing papers, but see [Hewitt and Liang](https://aclanthology.org/D19-1275/) for some thoughts on how to do probing, and e.g. [Voita et al.](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.14/) and [Pimentel et al.](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.420/) for other probing methods. Connecting more to the probing literature might help shed some light on important questions like: why do we do probing in the first place? What are we looking to find, and what would a new method have to bring, in order to be useful?
- I think the authors are much too sanguine re: the results of NeuroAI, and this shows in their review of prior work. Maybe be a bit more cautious in describing its putative successes.

questions.value: - Why do you refer to "neural topology"? I expected something about e.g. the topology of neural activations in the model, but it's actually just correlations between neurons over a given input.

Dear Reviewer SqX2,

Thank you for your prompt reply to our rebuttal and for acknowledging our efforts in strengthening the baselines and experimental results. We sincerely appreciate your willingness to raise your scores.


We understand your core concern: What does "neural topology" mean mechanistically, and how does it help us understand how LLMs actually work?

We would like to offer a perspective that might help clarify the "mental model" we are proposing.

1. **Mechanism: Topology as the Footprint of Functional Circuits.** You asked how the model "uses" the information encoded in the graph. We do not claim that the LLM explicitly computes a correlation matrix and reads it as a feature. Rather, the "neural topology" (correlation matrix) is a observable statistical footprint of active functional circuits. Traditional probing views representation as a static point in high-dimensional space (activation). Our work suggests viewing representation as a dynamic co-activation of neurons. The "graph" is simply a map of which neurons are working together (synchronizing) for the current input, capturing relationships that raw activations (magnitudes) miss. For example, two neurons might have the exact same average activation magnitude for two different inputs, but for Input A they fire together, and for Input B they fire independently. Our graph probe captures this structural distinction. In essense, the model "uses" the functional coupling (the circuit) to process information; the graph is simply our way of measuring which neurons are working together for a given input. However, we fully agree that it is extremely difficult to figure out the exact mechanisms behind these LLMs, via both activation and topology.

2. **Proof-of-Concept & Future Engineering.** We appreciate your recognition of our new baselines (WANDA, CCS, CRC, etc) and your valid point that our pruning experiments are proof-of-concept on smaller models. We agree that scaling this to larger models and more complex tasks is the necessary next step to fully operationalize this for engineering purposes.


We hope this clarifies that "neural topology" is not an arbitrary construct, but a statistical readout of the context-dependent functional connectivity of neural circuits. We believe this offers a novel and valuable lens for interpretability—moving from "which neurons are active?" to "which neurons are interacting?"

We are grateful for your time and constructive feedback, which has significantly improved the quality of this paper.


Sincerely,

The Authors

Dear Reviewer RV8o,

Thank you so much for your positive review. We sincerely appreciate the time you have taken to provide this feedback. We hope the following point-to-point response can address your remaining concerns.

---

**Q1.** Scalability of the technique.

**A1.** Thank you for your question regarding the scalability of our approach. We believe our method remains feasible for larger models for several reasons:

1.	**Layer-wise Construction:** Our graph construction operates within a single layer. The dimension $n$ corresponds to the hidden size of the model, not the total parameter count. For most current LLMs, including those up to 14B parameters (and even larger 70B models), the hidden size typically ranges from 4,096 to roughly 8,192 (often remaining below or near 5,000 for many models). An adjacency matrix of this size is computationally manageable, which explains why our approach scales efficiently to the 14B model in our experiments.
2.	**Sparsity and Compression:** As demonstrated in our sparsity experiments (Figure 3(a)), it is not necessary to store or process the complete dense $n \times n$ adjacency matrix. Our results verify that we can compress the graph by 10x or even 100x through sparsification keeping only the most significant edges without compromising the probing performance.
3.	**Strategies for Trillion-Parameter Scale:** We acknowledge that for trillion-parameter models where the hidden size might grow significantly larger, the computational burden could increase. However, we believe this can be effectively addressed through carefully calibrated techniques, such as neuron sampling, to approximate the topology without enumerating every connection.

---

**Q2.** Finetuning after pruning.

**A2.** Thank you for raising this really interesting point. In the scope of this work, we did not perform additional training or fine-tuning of the LLMs after pruning, primarily due to the expensive computational costs associated with training these large models. However, we completely agree that combining topological pruning with a brief re-tuning phase is an important future direction to explore. This step would likely be essential for effectively applying our proposed neural topology framework to real-world model compression and optimization applications.

**Q3.** Results on large LLMs.

**A3.** We apologize for any confusion regarding the presentation of our results on larger architectures. First, we would like to clarify that in our original submission, we did report probing results for LLMs ranging from 120M up to 14B parameters. Specifically, Figure 3B presents probing experiments on GPT-2-large (774M), Pythia-1.4B, Pythia-2.8B, Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B. These results confirm the consistent effectiveness of our proposed graph probing approach across this wide range of model sizes.

Second, to further address your concern and provide robust validation on large-scale models, we conducted additional interventional experiments on the Qwen2.5 family (3B, 7B, and 14B) during this rebuttal phase. These experiments extend the results originally presented in Section 4 (Figure 4c), which focused on 0.5B and 1.5B models. In this expanded analysis, we disabled 1% of neurons based on two criteria: Activation (magnitude) and Topology (degree, our method). We then compared the model performance on the MMLU benchmark. The results are summarized in the table below:


| LLM | Original Accuracy | Activation Intervention | Topology Intervention |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Qwen2.5-0.5B** | 0.4241 | 0.3305 | 0.2314 |
| **Qwen2.5-1.5B** | 0.5866 | 0.3352 | 0.2494 |
| **Qwen2.5-3B** | 0.6296 | 0.2584 | 0.2419 |
| **Qwen2.5-7B** | 0.6923 | 0.2562 | 0.2311 |
| **Qwen2.5-14B** | 0.7562 | 0.4865 | 0.2283 |

As shown in the table, intervention based on topology consistently incurs the largest performance drop across all scales, including the 14B model. This verifies the critical utility of neural topology in LLM computation and provides strong causal evidence regarding the model's reliance on these topological structures, even in larger architectures.

We hope this clarification and the additional experimental evidence address your concerns regarding the evaluation of large-scale models.

---

**Q4.** Functional specialization.

**A4.** Thank you so much for this keen observation regarding the high correlations observed in Figure 8b. We would like to address this from three perspectives:

1.	**Existence of a Stable Default Network:** We agree that the correlation values are uniformly high across different subjects. Far from contradicting our findings, this high baseline correlation is exactly what implies the existence of a stable "default network". It suggests that there is a robust, intrinsic topological structure in the LLM that persists regardless of the specific input prompt or subject matter. The "functional specification" we observe operates on top of this stable backbone.
2.	**Subtle Deviations and Human Brain Analogy:** While the differences are subtle, they are statistically meaningful and align with established findings in neuroscience. Specifically, Cole et al. (2014) demonstrated that in the human brain, task-evoked networks show strong correlations with the intrinsic (resting-state) network. Functional specialization often manifests as subtle reconfigurations of this stable architecture rather than a complete topological rewiring. The clustering we observe, even if subtle, indicates that the model consistently adapts this default network in subject-specific ways.
3.  **Average Smoothing:** It is also important to note that the correlation values in Figure 8b are calculated between the average topology of each subject. Averaging tends to smooth out noise and individual variations, naturally inflating correlation values. In our detailed analysis of individual pairs of neural topology (single prompt vs. single prompt), we found the correlations to be significantly lower, with the lowest values ranging between 0.5 and 0.7. This indicates that at the instance level, the functional specification is more distinct, while the average view highlights the consistent "default" structure shared across the model.

We sincerely hope the above explanations can address your concerns.

---

**Q5.** Mathematical definition of Neural Topology in Section 2 is incomplete.

**A5.** We apologize for the oversight regarding the notation in Section 2. You are entirely correct; in our formulation, $n$ represents the number of neurons, and $t$ denotes the number of input tokens (sequence length). We have revised the manuscript to explicitly define these symbols to ensure clarity and reproducibility.

Dear Reviewer SqX2,

Thank you again for your critical feedback regarding the need for robust baselines. We have continued working actively to address this concern and strengthen the validation of our method.

Over the last week, we successfully implemented and evaluated the very recent state-of-the-art approach, HaMI which is just published at NeurIPS 2025 (*Robust hallucination detection in llms via adaptive token selection.* Mengjia Niu, Hamed Haddadi, and Guansong Pang). We compared it against our Graph MLP probe alongside the previously added baselines (CCS and CRC). The updated results for hallucination detection are presented below:

| | CRC | 0.7420 |

| | **Graph MLP** | **0.8098** |
| **pythia-160m** | Activation MLP | 0.7751 |

| | HaMI | 0.7818 |
| | **Graph MLP** | **0.8166** |

**Key Finding:** Our topology-based approach consistently outperforms all three state-of-the-art baselines—including the cutting-edge HaMI method—across all tested models. This result strongly validates that neural topology captures distinct, high-quality signals for hallucination detection that are not fully exploited by existing activation-based methods.

We sincerely appreciate your push to incorporate these rigorous comparisons. With these additional experiments, we believe we have comprehensively addressed your concerns regarding evaluation standards. We are confident that the manuscript now meets and exceeds the bar for acceptance.

Sincerely,

The Authors

Thank you so much for your continued support and for recommending acceptance! We are glad that our clarifications and additional experiments satisfactorily addressed your questions. We sincerely appreciate the time and valuable feedback you have contributed throughout this review process, which has helped us strengthen our paper.

summary.value: This study proposes a novel method called Graph Probing, which analyzes the functional connectivity topology among neurons in LLMs to uncover its deep relationship with language generation performance. By adapting concepts from cognitive neuroscience, particularly functional connectivity and functional brain networks, the work introduces a fresh and innovative perspective to LLM interpretability. Empirical results reveal that LLMs exhibit stable default functional networks and hub neurons, and that the topological organization of these networks significantly influences model performance. The approach also shows promising potential for practical applications, such as model pruning, hallucination detection, and model fingerprinting.

strengths.value:
1.The integration of functional connectivity concepts from neuroscience into LLM analysis is conceptually innovative and may contribute to mechanistic interpretability.  
2.The authors have demonstrated that functional connectivity outperforms activation in predicting model performance, i.e., perplexity.
3.The authors have demonstrated the promising potential of “graph probing” for practical applications, such as model pruning, hallucination detection, and model fingerprinting.

weaknesses.value:
1.The manuscript is kind of overloaded while the validation of each point seems insufficient. 
2.Some interpretations of the results might be overstated.
3.Experimental results on large scale models is missing.

questions.value:
1.The manuscript is kind of overloaded. The authors tried to put too many points in one study, including graph probing, hub neurons, default network, functional specifications and three potential applications. All the points seem relate to “topology”. However, the limit of space makes the validation of each point to some extent insufficient. I would like to suggest the authors to focus on the main findings and elaborate experimental details, results and interpretations.
2.I am curious about the relationship between graph probing and hub neurons. In graph probing, it is practical to identify key connections that contribute significantly to the prediction of model performance (perplexity here). Are the neurons that constitute those important connections align with hub neurons? Or to what extent the nodes in important connections overlap with hub neurons?
3.All reported results are about small-scale LLMs. Given the focus on large models, results on at least 7B-class architectures are essential. Although the appendix mentions experiments on Qwen2.5-14B, no results, metrics, or analysis from this model are reported.   
4.About functional specification: Given extremely high correlation of neural topology (Figure 8b), I not very sure that this results show the functional specification or the default network. Actually, if you don’t put “law” in the middle, or apply a color bar with a wider range, probably the clustering effective would not be that clear.

Minor concerns:
1.The mathematical definition of Neural Topology in Section 2 is incomplete: key symbols such as n (neuron index?) and t (time step? input token?) are not defined, undermining clarity and reproducibility.  
2.A lot of the interpretation in the manuscript might be overstated. For example, but not being limited to:
“This remarkable stability confirms the existence of a default network in LLMs, where a fixed set of hub neurons play dominant roles regardless of the input, suggesting a fundamental organizing principle of their internal structure.” ---The DMN is a quite complex system in the brain. It’s functionality is far beyond “play dominant roles regardless of the input”.
“These findings strongly suggest that LLMs develop distinct and linearly separable topological patterns for different knowledge domains, allowing for easy extraction of the context or subject being processed.”---The experimental results do not support this claim. Separable topological patterns should be demonstrated before drawing such a strong conclusion.

summary.value:
The paper introduces graph probing, a probing method that treats an LLM’s neurons as nodes in a functional connectivity graph derived from token-time activation. Instead of probing raw activations, the method flattens the adjacency matrix of functional connectivity graph and trains lightweight MLP (and GNN) probes to predict LLM performance metrics such as perplexity. By probing models across diverse LLM families, the paper argues that the technique can predict next-token prediction performance using only neural topology.  They report gains up to 130%.

Beyond correlation, the paper probes causal structure in neural topology. It identifies a stable “default network” of high-degree hub neurons that recur across inputs, then shows that ablating only the top ~1% of degree-ranked neurons causes drastic MMLU accuracy drops.

Finally, the authors showcase practical applications of neural topology, including topology-informed pruning that removes many low-degree neurons with modest accuracy loss for downstream tasks.

strengths.value:
I find the paper well written and the empirical results are solid and sound. In terms of the main result, it shows neural topology probes reliably predict next-token performance and outperform activation-only baselines across multiple LLM families/sizes, with careful 8:2 train/test splits and standard regression metrics. The experimental setups are valid.

The paper also shows that the results are robust. In particular, performance persists under heavy graph sparsification and across model sizes and layers, suggesting the signal isn’t a fragile artifact of a single scale. 

Besides correlation, the paper offers a causal and interpretability perspective. The author(s) identify a stable “default network” of hub neurons and show that ablating the top 1% (by degree) yields large MMLU drops. This is stronger than random or activation-based selections, suggesting that models actually use this topology. These insights yield practical applications such as sparsity pruning and hallucination detection on TruthfulQA. 

The paper demonstrates that the technique is general. I appreciate the breath of the evaluations. It considers various model families and scales, including Qwen and Pythia series. In the appendix, it also describes experiments on VLMs by probing different sizes of LLaVA-v1.5. 

To my knowledge, the observations from the paper is novel and I believe it's a nice contribution.

weaknesses.value:
While the paper identifies a default network, I find it insufficient in explaining exactly what the network does. In addition, I'd love to see a mechanistic interpretation of “why” topology predicts performance.

If I understand correctly, building the per-sequence correlation graphs requires collecting full hidden-state time series and computing pairwise correlations, then training a probe. Although sparsification helps at inference time, the initial topology extraction can be costly in $n$ and $t$. How large is the computational overhead as we scale $n$ and $t$? Alternatively, it would be great to consider more efficient or approximate version of the algorithm.

Related to that, another minor concern is that the experiments of this paper top out at 14B parameter models. I am a bit worried about the computational cost of the technique. It would be nice to expand how much time / memory it would require to train & apply the probes as we scale model sizes. 

For the Truthful QA experiment, the inputs are constructed by concatenating each question with its true or false answer. In practice, users interact with LLM in a free form way. Could the paper clarify if the their method can help hallucination detection in a realistic setting?

questions.value:
I wonder how scalable the technique is. Specifically, the method requires you to construct a n by n adjacency graph. Would this still feasible for, say, trillion-parameter models?

For the pruning experiment, after removing low-degree neurons, did you try brief re-tuning (namely, a bit more fine-tuning) to recover accuracy?

In Appendix A.4, you used 10,000 random text sequences to construct neural connectivity graphs. I wonder if 10k is a universal constant that suffices for any models or scales, or if it should vary as well. In general, what is the sample complexity of training the graph probes? How many sequences are needed for the graph features to stabilize and the training loss of the probes to converge?

summary.value: This paper discusses probing LLMs to discover their underlying topology. While the paper is admittedly written well (according to the reviewers) an has certain good aspects about it, an important concern is that it does not situate itself well in relation to previous older (and not so older) work. There needs to be more such context in the paper that describes its relationship to older methods and other work that gives treatment to topology, especially based on the reviewer with the strongest position about the paper (see their specific references, but I feel it is a deeper issue than just adding a reference or two).

reviewer_scores.value: I don't know, though it sounds like one reviewer did increase their score before the regression to the older scores.

comment.value:
Thanks for the thorough response! Here are my thoughts:

> The primary contribution of our paper is to propose a new "object" for analysis: neural topology, distinct from the traditional focus on neural activation. While standard probing links activations to semantics, our goal is to demonstrate that the interactions between neurons (the dynamic graph structure) contain unique, high-level information that raw activations alone do not capture.

This is helpful context! I think one thing that is confusing to me is what neural topology is supposed to mean, mechanistically. Sure, you can extract information from this correlation matrix that you cannot extract from a last-token representation, or mean of token representations. But there are probably other functions of a model's set of representations (taken over time) that also might do a better job of preserving information at all positions of a sentence than averages or last-tokens. 

Why is topology (defined as you do) a natural / useful way of looking at LLM neurons? What are the mechanisms by which models might actually use information encoded in the way you suggest? Without this understanding of what neural topology  means for LLMs, I struggle to convince myself that it's really a meaningful object of study.

Fundamentally, I don't feel that this construct helps me understand better either LLM mechanisms or representations; it's not clear to me how I should update my mental model of how LLMs work.

> (updated experiments with baselines)... We do not claim that a simple topological probe establishes a new state-of-the-art for every distinct task. Rather, these experiments serve as proof-of-concept demonstrations. They are designed to show that neural topology contains rich, exploitable information that is distinct from raw activations.

Thanks for providing these baselines! These really help confirm that the probes work reasonably well. Realistically, there are still issues with these - you're comparing to Wanda on models that are too small to warrant pruning, on tasks that they don't study, for example - but I appreciate that you've done them. 

This said, I don't really think that these proof-of-concept demonstrations help this paper from an interpretability point of view. While standard probing uses a (linear) model to extract information from model activations, something which clearly corresponds to a mechanism that LLMs (could) use, I don't really know what this graph object corresponds to, or if it has any relation at all to the mechanisms used by LLMs.

As such, I am ultimately still against the acceptance of this paper. I think that more work is needed to clarify how models would / could / do use the information encoded in these graph objects. However, the authors have done an admirable job of shoring up the deficiencies in the initial draft, and as such I will update my soundness score; I will also change my overall score to 4 (though frankly I would choose a 3, if that were an option).

**Q3.** Relation to Prior Work

**A3.** We sincerely thank the reviewer for the detailed list of valuable references and for identifying the gaps in our literature review. We agree that contextualizing our findings within the broader history of interpretability and probing is essential for the paper's quality. We will make sure to include all the suggested papers and additional relevant works in the final manuscript to provide a comprehensive and accurate landscape of the field.

---

**Q4.** Why do you refer to "neural topology"?

**A4.** Thank you for raising this point about our terminology. We chose the term "neural topology" to explicitly emphasize the functional and topological connectivity between neurons, rather than just their static weights or instantaneous activation values.

This terminology is directly inspired by neuroscience, particularly studies of the human brain. In that field, researchers often distinguish between structural connectivity (physical wiring) and functional connectivity (statistical dependencies or correlations between regions). The organization of these functional connections—how they form clusters, hubs, and efficient information pathways—is widely referred to as the network's "topology" (e.g., small-world topology).

By adopting this term, we aim to highlight that we are analyzing the LLM as a dynamic graph where the pattern of interactions (correlations) defines the computational structure processing the input. However, we apologize for any confusion this naming choice may have caused. We are flexible regarding the terminology and are fully open to changing the name according to your suggestions to ensure the utmost clarity for the readers.


---

Thank you once again for your invaluable guidance throughout this process which has been instrumental in strengthening our work. We hope that with these clarifications and the additional experiments, you might agree it now meets the bar for acceptance. We would be deeply grateful if you would consider an increase to your score.


Sincerely,

The Authors
Thank you for clarifications and sharing the new experiments! I maintain my rating and will recommend accept to the AC.

**Q3.** Dataset size.

**A3.** Thank you for this important question regarding the data requirements for our method. Fundamentally, our graph probing framework behaves as a standard graph regression or classification task, whether utilizing simple linear/MLP probes or more complex GNN probes. In our experience across various tasks, training these probes typically requires only a few thousand samples to achieve convergence and stable performance.

To illustrate this with specific examples from our submission:
- Perplexity Regression: We utilized 10,000 samples, which proved sufficient for high-accuracy prediction.
- Hallucination Detection: The dataset contained 5,918 samples, and our method was able to learn effective decision boundaries with this amount of data.


Furthermore, during this rebuttal phase, we conducted additional experiments to test the robustness of our method with larger datasets. We utilized datasets concerning historical artworks and world places for time and space regression tasks, respectively, which contain approximately 30,000 samples. Dear Area Chairs and Reviewers,

We sincerely thank the reviewers (RV8o, SqX2, TRCD) for their constructive feedback and engagement. Based on their suggestions, we have significantly strengthened the manuscript with new baselines, large-scale experiments, and deeper mechanistic investigations. We are pleased that Reviewer RV8o has **recommended acceptance (Score: 8)** and Reviewer SqX2 **raised their score** acknowledging our improvements. Below is a summary of the key revisions and new experimental evidence provided during the discussion phase:

1. **Causal Mechanism of Neural Topology (Addressing Reviewer SqX2’s Core Concern)**. Reviewer SqX2 questioned the mechanistic validity of our approach, specifically asking how specific neuron-neuron interactions drive model behavior. To address this, we conducted a new **"minimal intervention"** experiment. Instead of global pruning, we surgically disabled the interactions of only one or two specific neurons (Top-1/2 vs. Bottom-1/2 degree). We find that disabling the interaction of a single hub neuron in Qwen2.5-0.5B caused the loss to explode **from 2.9182 to 4.7223** (a >1000x increase in loss increment compared to non-hub neurons), which provides striking causal evidence that the topological connections identified by our method are not merely correlational byproducts, but load-bearing functional pathways essential for model computation.

2. **Expanded Baselines and Stronger Evaluation (Addressing SqX2 and TRCD)**. We addressed concerns regarding insufficient baselines by incorporating state-of-the-art comparisons across all applications. For **model pruning**, we compared against **WANDA (ICLR 2024)**. Our topological pruning significantly outperforms WANDA, retaining ~51% accuracy vs. WANDA’s ~30% on Qwen2.5-1.5B (25% pruning ratio). For **hallucination detection**, we added **CCS and CRC (ICLR 2023)**. Our method consistently achieves higher detection accuracy. For **probing**, we added an "average activation" baseline. Graph probing still consistently outperforms it, confirming that structural connectivity contains information beyond aggregate activation magnitude.

3. **Generalization to New Semantics: Space and Time (Addressing SqX2 and TRCD)**. To demonstrate utility beyond perplexity, we adopted the space/time datasets from **Gurnee & Tegmark (2024)**. Graph probing significantly outperforms activation baselines in predicting the release time of artworks and coordinates of world places (e.g., >40% improvement in MSE for Qwen2.5), validating that neural topology captures rich, interpretable semantic information.

4. **Scalability to Large Models (Addressing TRCD and RV8o)**. We addressed concerns about model scale by extending our interventional experiments to the **Qwen2.5-14B** model. Interventional experiments confirm that topological importance remains a critical predictor of performance even at the 14B scale, with topological pruning causing the most significant performance drops compared to activation-based methods.

5. **Clarifications and Refinements**. We clarified that our layer-wise construction scales with hidden size ($d$), not parameter count, making it feasible for large models. In addition, we corrected mathematical notations in Section 2. Furthermore, we tuned down biological analogies (e.g., default mode network) to focus on the empirical stability of hub neurons.


We believe these extensive additions have resolved the reviewers' concerns regarding the mechanism, utility, and robustness of neural topology. We are confident that this work now offers a novel and rigorously validated lens for understanding LLMs' internal structure.

Thank you again for acknowledging our work and rebuttal! Special thanks to Reviewer RV8o for their continuous support and recommendation to acceptance.

Sincerely,

The Authors

> Mechanism: Topology as the Footprint of Functional Circuits. You asked how the model "uses" the information encoded in the graph. We do not claim that the LLM explicitly computes a correlation matrix and reads it as a feature. Rather, the "neural topology" (correlation matrix) is a observable statistical footprint of active functional circuits. Traditional probing views representation as a static point in high-dimensional space (activation). Our work suggests viewing representation as a dynamic co-activation of neurons. The "graph" is simply a map of which neurons are working together (synchronizing) for the current input, capturing relationships that raw activations (magnitudes) miss. For example, two neurons might have the exact same average activation magnitude for two different inputs, but for Input A they fire together, and for Input B they fire independently. Our graph probe captures this structural distinction. In essense, the model "uses" the functional coupling (the circuit) to process information; the graph is simply our way of measuring which neurons are working together for a given input. However, we fully agree that it is extremely difficult to figure out the exact mechanisms behind these LLMs, via both activation and topology.

Thanks! This doesn't quite answer my question. I think, contrary to your last assertion, that we have a rather good idea of what traditional activation-space probes measure, and the mechanisms by which models could / do use the information that they probe for. Since probes just find a linear direction in activation space, transformer LLMs can directly read in from that direction, and avail themselves of that information. 

On the other hand, as you say, it seems unlikely that models actually compute a correlation matrix, so they probably don't actually have access to the information that your probes use. Indeed, while these correlations may be downstream of some mechanism that could be worth studying, there is no clear connection between the correlations themselves and the model's mechanisms. It is for this reason that I feel that these graph probes provide a limited contribution to the interpretability literature: it's not clear what any results derived from graph probing can tell us about the models they seek to explain. 

I understand your interest in "moving from "which neurons are active?" to "which neurons are interacting?"", but I think this would be more effectively done by finding a mechanism by which a specific neuron-neuron interaction drives model behavior, than by computing correlation matrices that capture neuron-neuron interactions, but do not explain how these could arise or affect model behavior.

**Clarification on Scope:** Finally, we would like to clarify the intended scope of these experiments. Domains like model pruning and hallucination detection are highly specialized fields with extensive literature. We do not claim that a simple topological probe establishes a new state-of-the-art for every distinct task. Rather, these experiments serve as proof-of-concept demonstrations. They are designed to show that neural topology contains rich, exploitable information that is distinct from raw activations. We hope these results encourage the community to view neural topology as a valuable new dimension for optimizing and interpreting LLMs.
